title: Oracle SQL Reviewer Question Bank 201-249
description: Structured question bank for Practice Mode and 63-question Mock Exam generation. Official scoring follows the document-highlighted answers.

questions.stem: Which three SQL statements display the value 1890.55 as $1,890.55?

sections.title: Required output
sections.content:
$1,890.55
The format must include a dollar sign, a thousands separator, and exactly two decimal places.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9G999D00') FROM dual;
options.explanation: $ displays the currency symbol, G displays the group separator, and D00 displays the decimal separator followed by two digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9,999V99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: V scales the number rather than displaying a decimal separator, so it does not produce the required currency format.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$00G000D00') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The format includes a currency symbol, group separator, decimal separator, and two required decimal digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$99,999D99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: This format includes extra leading digit positions and uses mixed literal and NLS-sensitive separators, so it is not one of the document’s marked answers.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(1890.55, '$9G999D99') FROM dual;
options.explanation: G and D use the applicable NLS group and decimal characters, while 99 displays the two decimal digits.

questions.answerExplanation: $ displays the currency symbol, G displays the group separator, and D00 displays the decimal separator followed by two digits. The format includes a currency symbol, group separator, decimal separator, and two required decimal digits. G and D use the applicable NLS group and decimal characters, while 99 displays the two decimal digits.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about self-joins?

options.text: They require the EXISTS operator in the join condition.
options.explanation: A self-join normally relates two aliases of the same table using a standard join condition. EXISTS is not required.

options.text: They have no join condition.
options.explanation: A meaningful self-join normally has a condition that relates rows from the two references to the same table.

options.text: They require the NOT EXISTS operator in the join condition.
options.explanation: NOT EXISTS is not a requirement for a self-join.

options.text: They require table aliases.
options.explanation: Separate aliases distinguish the two references to the same table and allow their columns to be qualified.

options.text: They are always equijoins.
options.explanation: A self-join can use equality, inequality, range, inner-join, or outer-join conditions.

options.text: They can use INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.
options.explanation: A self-join may be implemented using inner-join or outer-join syntax, depending on the required result.

questions.answerExplanation: Separate aliases distinguish the two references to the same table and allow their columns to be qualified. A self-join may be implemented using inner-join or outer-join syntax, depending on the required result.

questions.stem: A subquery is called a single-row subquery when ________.

options.text: There is only one subquery in the outer query and the inner query returns one or more values.
options.explanation: The number of subqueries in the outer query does not determine whether a subquery is a single-row subquery.

options.text: The inner query returns a single value to the outer query.
options.explanation: A single-row subquery returns no more than one row to the parent statement and is commonly used with single-row comparison operators.

options.text: The inner query uses an aggregating function and returns one or more values.
options.explanation: An aggregate function may return one value, but using an aggregate function is not the defining requirement.

options.text: The inner query returns one or more values and the outer query returns a single value.
options.explanation: The outer query’s result size does not define the inner query as a single-row subquery.

questions.answerExplanation: A single-row subquery returns no more than one row to the parent statement and is commonly used with single-row comparison operators.

questions.stem: You must write a query that prompts for column names and conditions every time it is executed. The user must be prompted only once for the table name. Which statement achieves these objectives?

sections.title: Requirement
sections.content:
Prompt every execution for both column names and the condition.
A single & is used for repeated prompting, while && defines and retains the table-name substitution variable.
Prompt only once for the table name and retain that value.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &table WHERE &condition = '&cond';
options.explanation: The table variable uses a single &, so it is not automatically retained for later execution.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM '&table' WHERE &condition = &cond;
options.explanation: Single quotation marks turn the table substitution into character text rather than a valid table identifier.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &&table WHERE &condition = '&cond';
options.explanation: &col1, &col2, &condition, and &cond prompt when undefined. &&table prompts once and defines the table variable for reuse.

options.text: SELECT &col1, &col2 FROM &&table WHERE &condition = &&cond;
options.explanation: &&cond retains the condition value, but the requirement says that the condition value should be prompted every time.

questions.answerExplanation: &col1, &col2, &condition, and &cond prompt when undefined. &&table prompts once and defines the table variable for reuse.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true regarding single-row functions?

options.text: The data type returned can be different from the data type of the referenced argument.
options.explanation: Conversion functions can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a number or date to character data.

options.text: They can return multiple values for more than one data type.
options.explanation: A single-row function returns one result for each input row.

options.text: They can accept only one argument.
options.explanation: Some functions accept one argument, while others accept two or more.

options.text: They can be nested only to two levels.
options.explanation: Single-row functions can be nested beyond two levels when the returned data types remain compatible.

options.text: They can be used in SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY clauses.
options.explanation: Single-row functions can calculate displayed values, filter rows, and provide sort expressions.

options.text: They can accept column names, expressions, variable names, or user-supplied constants as arguments.
options.explanation: Function arguments may include columns, literals, variables, and valid expressions.

questions.answerExplanation: Conversion functions can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a number or date to character data. Single-row functions can calculate displayed values, filter rows, and provide sort expressions. Function arguments may include columns, literals, variables, and valid expressions.

questions.stem: Examine the DEPARTMENTS table and the compound query. Which two ORDER BY clauses can be used to sort the output?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT dep_name, 'b'
FROM departments
WHERE department_id = 90
UNION
SELECT department_id, department_name DEPT_NAME, 'a'
FROM departments
WHERE department_id = 10;

options.text: ORDER BY DEPT_NAME;
options.explanation: This is not one of the choices marked as valid in the document.

options.text: ORDER BY DEPT_ID;
options.explanation: The document marks the department-ID output alias as valid for sorting the compound result.

options.text: ORDER BY 'b';
options.explanation: 'b' is a constant character literal, not an output column reference for meaningful sorting.

options.text: ORDER BY 3;
options.explanation: A final ORDER BY can refer to a result column by its ordinal position.

questions.answerExplanation: The document marks the department-ID output alias as valid for sorting the compound result. A final ORDER BY can refer to a result column by its ordinal position.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the WHERE and HAVING clauses in a SELECT statement?

options.text: The WHERE and HAVING clauses can be used in the same statement only if they are applied to different columns.
options.explanation: The clauses can reference the same column when appropriate. Their distinction is based on when filtering occurs.

options.text: Aggregate functions and columns used in HAVING must be specified in the query’s SELECT list.
options.explanation: An aggregate expression can be used in HAVING without being displayed in the select list.

options.text: The WHERE clause can exclude rows after dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

options.text: The HAVING clause can be used with aggregate functions in subqueries.
options.explanation: A subquery may group rows and use HAVING to filter its aggregate results.

options.text: The WHERE clause can exclude rows before dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: Rows rejected by WHERE do not participate in the later grouping and aggregate calculations.

questions.answerExplanation: A subquery may group rows and use HAVING to filter its aggregate results. Rows rejected by WHERE do not participate in the later grouping and aggregate calculations.

questions.stem: You must create an EMPLOYEES table. EMPLOYEE_ID, EMPLOYEE_NAME, LOYEES_ID, and LOGIN_ID must be unique and not null. Which two statements create the required table?

sections.title: Requirements
items: The specified identifier and login columns must reject nulls and duplicate values.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A composite unique constraint permits multiple rows containing null components and does not individually make both columns non-null.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(25), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_pk PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A composite primary key makes both key columns unique as a combination and implicitly NOT NULL.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT emp_id_pk PRIMARY KEY, login_id NUMBER UNIQUE, employee_name VARCHAR2(25), hire_date DATE);
options.explanation: The unique constraint on LOGIN_ID permits nulls unless NOT NULL is also declared.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER, login_id NUMBER, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id), CONSTRAINT emp_id_nn NOT NULL (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: A NOT NULL constraint cannot be declared as a table-level constraint over multiple columns using this syntax.

options.text: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT emp_id_nn NOT NULL, login_id NUMBER CONSTRAINT login_id_nn NOT NULL, employee_name VARCHAR2(100), hire_date DATE, CONSTRAINT emp_num_id_uk UNIQUE (employee_id, login_id));
options.explanation: Both columns are explicitly NOT NULL, and the composite UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate employee-and-login combinations.

questions.answerExplanation: A composite primary key makes both key columns unique as a combination and implicitly NOT NULL. Both columns are explicitly NOT NULL, and the composite UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate employee-and-login combinations.

questions.stem: In your session, NLS_DATE_FORMAT is set to DD-MON-RR. Which two queries display the year as four digits?

sections.title: Session setting
sections.content:
NLS_DATE_FORMAT = 'DD-MON-RR'
The session’s default display uses a two-digit RR year unless an explicit four-digit format is applied.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(SYSDATE, 'RRRR-MM-DD') FROM dual;
options.explanation: SYSDATE is already a date. TO_DATE does not format a date for display and introduces an unnecessary implicit conversion.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'MM/DD/YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: YYYY explicitly formats the year using four digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6), 'dd-mon-yyyy') FROM dual;
options.explanation: ADD_MONTHS already returns a date, and TO_DATE is not the correct function for formatting it for display.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6)) FROM dual;
options.explanation: Without an explicit format model, the conversion uses the session’s DD-MON-RR setting and displays a two-digit year.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, 6), 'dd-mon-yyyy') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The explicit YYYY format element displays the year as four digits.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'MM/DD/YYYY'), 'MM/DD/YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The final result is a DATE, whose display again follows NLS_DATE_FORMAT, which uses a two-digit year.

questions.answerExplanation: YYYY explicitly formats the year using four digits. The explicit YYYY format element displays the year as four digits.

questions.stem: A non-correlated subquery can be defined as __________.

options.text: A set of sequential queries in which the result of the inner query is used as the search value in the outer query.
options.explanation: A non-correlated subquery executes independently, and its result is supplied to the outer query.

options.text: A set of sequential queries, all of which must return values from the same table.
options.explanation: The subquery and outer query may retrieve data from different tables.

options.text: A set of sequential queries, all of which must always return a single value.
options.explanation: A non-correlated subquery may return one row, multiple rows, or no rows, depending on how it is used.

options.text: A SELECT statement that can be embedded only in a clause of another SELECT statement.
options.explanation: Subqueries may also be used in DML and other supported SQL statements.

questions.answerExplanation: A non-correlated subquery executes independently, and its result is supplied to the outer query.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the USING clause when joining tables?

options.text: It is used to specify an equijoin of columns that have the same name in both tables.
options.explanation: USING(column_name) creates an equality comparison between same-named columns in the joined tables.

options.text: It is used to specify an explicit join condition involving operators.
options.explanation: Arbitrary conditions and operators are specified with an ON clause.

options.text: It can never be used with natural joins.
options.explanation: This statement is not highlighted as correct in the document.

options.text: It can never be used with a full outer join.
options.explanation: A full outer join may use USING when the joining columns have the same name.

options.text: All column names in a USING clause must be qualified with a table name or table alias.
options.explanation: This statement is highlighted as correct in the document.

questions.answerExplanation: USING(column_name) creates an equality comparison between same-named columns in the joined tables. This statement is highlighted as correct in the document.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true regarding subqueries?

options.text: A main query can have many subqueries.
options.explanation: One parent statement can contain multiple subqueries in supported clauses and expressions.

options.text: A subquery can have more than one main query.
options.explanation: A subquery belongs to its containing parent query or statement.

options.text: The subquery and main query must retrieve data from the same table.
options.explanation: The inner and outer queries may retrieve data from different tables.

options.text: The subquery and main query can retrieve data from different tables.
options.explanation: The tables referenced by the inner and outer queries do not have to be the same.

options.text: Only one column or expression can be compared between the subquery and main query.
options.explanation: Oracle supports multiple-column subqueries and row-value comparisons.

options.text: Multiple columns or expressions can be compared between the subquery and main query.
options.explanation: Compatible combinations of columns or expressions may be compared between the query blocks.

questions.answerExplanation: One parent statement can contain multiple subqueries in supported clauses and expressions. The tables referenced by the inner and outer queries do not have to be the same. Compatible combinations of columns or expressions may be compared between the query blocks.

questions.stem: Examine the PROMOTIONS table and the SQL statement. What is the outcome?

sections.title: Requirement
sections.content: Find the average promotion cost for category A in the ranges $0–2000 and $2001–5000.

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT AVG(CASE
WHEN promo_cost BETWEEN 0 AND 2000
AND promo_category = 'A'
THEN promo_cost
ELSE NULL
END) "CAT_2000A",
AVG(CASE
WHEN promo_cost BETWEEN 2001 AND 5000
AND promo_category = 'A'
THEN promo_cost
ELSE NULL
END) "CAT_5000A"
FROM promotions;

options.text: It generates an error because multiple conditions cannot be specified for the WHEN clause.
options.explanation: Multiple conditions can be combined with AND in a searched CASE expression.

options.text: It executes successfully and gives the required result.
options.explanation: Each CASE returns PROMO_COST for its specified range and category. AVG ignores the null results and calculates each conditional average.

options.text: It generates an error because CASE cannot be used with group functions.
options.explanation: A CASE expression can be used as the argument of an aggregate function.

options.text: It generates an error because NULL cannot be specified as a return value.
options.explanation: A CASE expression may return null, and AVG ignores null values.

questions.answerExplanation: Each CASE returns PROMO_COST for its specified range and category. AVG ignores the null results and calculates each conditional average.

questions.stem: Examine the ORDER_ITEMS table. Which two queries return rows where QUANTITY is a multiple of ten?

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity = TRUNC(quantity, -1);
options.explanation: This statement is not highlighted as correct in the document.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity / 10 = TRUNC(quantity);
options.explanation: Dividing the quantity by ten and comparing it with the original truncated quantity does not test whether the quantity is divisible by ten.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE FLOOR(quantity / 10) = TRUNC(quantity);
options.explanation: This statement is highlighted as correct in the document.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE quantity = ROUND(quantity, 1);
options.explanation: Integer quantities remain unchanged when rounded to one decimal place, even when they are not multiples of ten.

options.text: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE MOD(quantity, 10) = 0;
options.explanation: A quantity is divisible by ten when division by ten leaves a remainder of zero.

questions.answerExplanation: This statement is highlighted as correct in the document. A quantity is divisible by ten when division by ten leaves a remainder of zero.

questions.stem: Examine the query below, which executes successfully. What is the result?

codeBlocks.title: Query

options.text: It returns rows that are not common to both SELECT statements.
options.explanation: This describes a difference operation, not UNION ALL.

options.text: It returns rows from both SELECT statements after eliminating duplicate rows.
options.explanation: UNION removes duplicate rows, while UNION ALL retains them.

options.text: It returns rows common to both SELECT statements.
options.explanation: This describes INTERSECT.

options.explanation: UNION ALL combines all rows without performing duplicate elimination.

questions.answerExplanation: UNION ALL combines all rows without performing duplicate elimination.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true regarding multiple-row subqueries?

options.text: They can contain group functions.
options.explanation: A multiple-row subquery can use aggregate functions, often together with grouping, to return multiple aggregate results.

options.text: They always contain a subquery within a subquery.
options.explanation: A multiple-row subquery does not require another nested subquery.

options.text: They use the < ALL operator to imply less than the maximum.
options.explanation: < ALL means less than every returned value, which normally means less than the minimum returned value.

options.text: They can be used to retrieve multiple rows from a single table only.
options.explanation: Multiple-row subqueries may retrieve data from joins, views, or other supported row sources.

options.text: They should not be used with the NOT IN operator in the main query if NULL is likely to be part of the subquery result.
options.explanation: If the subquery result contains null, a NOT IN comparison can evaluate to unknown and return no rows unexpectedly.

questions.answerExplanation: A multiple-row subquery can use aggregate functions, often together with grouping, to return multiple aggregate results. If the subquery result contains null, a NOT IN comparison can evaluate to unknown and return no rows unexpectedly.

questions.stem: Examine the CUSTOMERS and CUST_HISTORY tables. You need to find customers who have never changed their address. Which set operator should be used?

sections.title: Required result
sections.content: Return current customers who do not appear in the address-change history.

options.text: INTERSECT
options.explanation: INTERSECT returns rows appearing in both query results.

options.text: UNION ALL
options.explanation: UNION ALL combines both result sets and keeps duplicate rows.

options.text: MINUS
options.explanation: MINUS returns rows from the first result that are not present in the second result.

options.text: UNION
options.explanation: UNION combines both results and removes duplicates rather than subtracting historical customers.

questions.answerExplanation: MINUS returns rows from the first result that are not present in the second result.

questions.stem: Examine the PRODUCTS and ORDER_ITEMS tables and the query below. What happens when the statement is executed?

sections.title: Expected output
sections.content:
PRODUCT_NAME │ ITEM_CNT
The product with no order-item row is still returned with a null count.

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT p.product_name, i.item_cnt
FROM (
SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) item_cnt
 FROM order_items
GROUP BY product_id
) i RIGHT OUTER JOIN products p
ON i.product_id = p.product_id;

options.text: The statement executes successfully and produces the required output.
options.explanation: Inline views can be used with outer joins, the alias ITEM_CNT is available to the outer query, and grouping is allowed inside the inline view.

options.text: The statement does not execute because inline views and outer joins cannot be used together.
options.explanation: An inline view can participate in an outer join.

options.text: The statement does not execute because the ITEM_CNT alias cannot be displayed in the outer query.
options.explanation: An inline-view column alias can be referenced by the outer query.

options.text: The statement does not execute because GROUP BY cannot be used in the inline view.
options.explanation: An inline view may contain GROUP BY and aggregate functions.

questions.answerExplanation: Inline views can be used with outer joins, the alias ITEM_CNT is available to the outer query, and grouping is allowed inside the inline view.

options.explanation: Corresponding null values participate when UNION compares complete rows and eliminates duplicates.

options.explanation: Corresponding columns need compatible data types, but their names do not have to be identical.

questions.stem: You issued the following command: DROP TABLE employees; Which three statements are true?

options.text: All uncommitted transactions are committed.
options.explanation: DROP TABLE is a DDL statement, so Oracle implicitly commits the current transaction.

options.text: All indexes and constraints defined on the table being dropped are also dropped.
options.explanation: The indexes and constraints belonging to the table are removed with the table.

options.text: Sequences used in the EMPLOYEES table become invalid.
options.explanation: Sequences are independent schema objects and remain valid after the table is dropped.

options.text: The space used by the EMPLOYEES table is reclaimed immediately.
options.explanation: Without PURGE, an eligible table may be retained in the recycle bin.

options.text: The EMPLOYEES table can be recovered using the ROLLBACK command.
options.explanation: DROP TABLE cannot be reversed using ROLLBACK. An eligible table may instead be recovered using Flashback Drop.

options.text: The EMPLOYEES table is moved to the recycle bin.
options.explanation: Without PURGE, an eligible dropped table is moved to the recycle bin.

questions.answerExplanation: DROP TABLE is a DDL statement, so Oracle implicitly commits the current transaction. The indexes and constraints belonging to the table are removed with the table. Without PURGE, an eligible dropped table is moved to the recycle bin.

questions.stem: Examine the CREATE TABLE statements for the STORES and SALES tables. The DELETE statement fails with ORA-02292. Which three options ensure that the statement executes successfully?

sections.content:
sales_id NUMBER(4) CONSTRAINT sales_id_pk PRIMARY KEY,
 item_id NUMBER(4),
 quantity NUMBER(10),
 sales_date DATE,
 store_id NUMBER(4),
 CONSTRAINT store_id_fk FOREIGN KEY (store_id)
 REFERENCES stores(store_id)
);

sections.title: Error
sections.content:
ORA-02292: integrity constraint (HR.STORE_ID_FK) violated
A child row in SALES references store 900.

options.text: Disable the primary key in the STORES table.
options.explanation: This does not properly remove the child rows that reference the parent row.

options.text: Use the CASCADE keyword with the DELETE statement.
options.explanation: Oracle does not support a general DELETE ... CASCADE clause in this form.

options.text: Delete the rows with STORE_ID = 900 from the SALES table and then delete the row from the STORES table.
options.explanation: Removing the dependent child rows first allows the parent row to be deleted.

options.text: Disable the foreign key in the SALES table and then delete the row.
options.explanation: Oracle will not enforce the foreign-key relationship while the constraint is disabled.

options.text: Create the foreign key in the SALES table on SALES_ID with the ON DELETE CASCADE option.
options.explanation: This is marked as correct in the document image.

questions.answerExplanation: Removing the dependent child rows first allows the parent row to be deleted. Oracle will not enforce the foreign-key relationship while the constraint is disabled. This is marked as correct in the document image.

questions.stem: In the CUSTOMERS table, CUST_CITY contains Paris for CUST_FIRST_NAME Abigail. Evaluate the query. What is the outcome?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT INITCAP(cust_first_name || ' ' ||
UPPER(SUBSTR(cust_city, -LENGTH(cust_city), 2)))
FROM customers
WHERE cust_first_name = 'Abigail';

options.text: Abigail Pa
options.explanation: The outer INITCAP converts the intermediate value Abigail PA to Abigail Pa.

options.text: Abigail PA
options.explanation: This is the value before the outer INITCAP function is applied.

options.text: Abigail IS
options.explanation: The expression extracts the first two characters of Paris, not the last two.

options.text: An error message
options.explanation: The character functions and concatenation are valid.

questions.answerExplanation: The outer INITCAP converts the intermediate value Abigail PA to Abigail Pa.

questions.stem: You notice a performance change in your production Oracle 12c database. You want to know which change caused this performance difference. Which method or feature should you use?

options.text: Compare Period ADDM report.
options.explanation: This is not the answer highlighted in the source document.
